For a probability kernel $P$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $D$ is **petite** if there are a probability measure $\nu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), nonnegative weights $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\sum_{n\ge1}a_n=1$, and a constant $\alpha>0$ such that
$$\sum_{n\ge1}a_nP^n(x,A)\ge\alpha\nu(A)\quad(x\in D,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
This is a randomized-time minorization. A small set requires one fixed time; a petite set permits a common distribution over positive integer times.

For a probability kernel $P$ on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), a measurable set $C$ is **$(m,\epsilon,\nu)$-small** if $m\ge1$ is an integer, $0<\epsilon\le1$, $\nu$ is a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]), and
$$P^m(x,A)\ge\epsilon\nu(A)\quad(x\in C,\ A\in\mathcal X).$$
The inequality is pointwise in $x$ and holds for every measurable $A$.

A **geometric drift inequality outside $C$** consists of a finite-valued measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,\infty)$, constants $0<\lambda<1$ and $0\le b<\infty$, and
$$PV(x):=\int V(y)P(x,dy)\le\lambda V(x)+b\,1_C(x)\quad(x\in\mathsf X).$$
The terms small set and drift are separate hypotheses; neither definition asserts the existence of the other.

When an invariant probability $\pi$ is specified ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), an **extended geometric drift certificate finite $\pi$-almost everywhere** allows measurable $V:\mathsf X\to[1,+\infty]$ with $\pi(V<\infty)=1$ and the same pointwise inequality, interpreted in the nonnegative extended reals. This is a separate convention from the finite-valued drift function above. The geometric theorem treats this certificate on $E=\{V<\infty\}$; the original finite-valued convention gives the corresponding bound on the whole state space.

Let $P$ be $\phi$-irreducible ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]) and aperiodic ([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $
u\ll\pi$ be a probability. Suppose every state has some $n(x)\ge1$ and $\delta(x)>0$ with $P^{n(x)}(x,\cdot)\ge\delta(x)
u(\cdot)$. Then there is $N$ such that for every $n\ge N$, $
u P^n\ge\epsilon_n
u$ for some $\epsilon_n>0$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a countably generated measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), $P$ a probability kernel ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and $\phi$ a nonzero $\sigma$-finite measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) on $\mathcal X$. Write $P^n$ for the $n$-fold kernel iterate. The kernel is **$\phi$-irreducible** if, for every $A\in\mathcal X$ with $\phi(A)>0$ and every $x\in\mathsf X$, there is an integer $n\ge1$ such that $P^n(x,A)>0$. Equivalently, the sum of these nonnegative probabilities over $n\ge1$ is positive. No recurrence or invariant law is part of this definition.

Assume Choice. Let $X$ be a $K$-chain, let
$\tau:\Omega\to\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ be a stopping time, and let $H$ be a
bounded measurable path functional. Put $h(x)=\mathbb E_xH$ and define the
everywhere meaningful random variables
$$ Z_H:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}H(X_n,X_{n+1},\ldots), \qquad R_h:=\sum_{n\ge0}1_{\{\tau=n\}}h(X_n). $$ Both are defined to be zero on $\{\tau=\infty\}$. Then $$ \mathbb E[Z_H\mid\mathcal F_\tau]=R_h\quad\text{a.s.} $$ This is the precise meaning of the usual eventwise notation $$ \mathbb E[1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}H(X_\tau,X_{\tau+1},\ldots)\mid\mathcal F_\tau] =1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}h(X_\tau): $$
no value $X_\infty$ is used. If $\tau<\infty$ almost surely, the indicators can
be omitted.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim:
The petite inequality on $C$ gives $\sum_na_nP^n(x,C)\ge\alpha
u(C)>0$ for every $x\in D$. Choose $M$ so $\sum_{n>M}a_n<\alpha
u(C)/2$. Since $P^n(x,C)\le\Pr_x(	au_C\le n)\le\Pr_x(	au_C\le M)$ for $n\le M$, the truncated weighted sum gives $\Pr_x(	au_C\le M)\ge q:=\alpha
u(C)/2$ uniformly on $D$.

Since $
u(C)>0$ and $
u\ll\pi$, $\pi(C)>0$. To see that every state has positive probability of reaching $C$, let $H=\{x\in C^c:P^n(x,C)=0	ext{ for every }n\ge1\}$. Kernel iteration makes $H$ measurable. If $x\in H$ and $P(x,H^c)>0$, the countable union $H^c=C\cup igcup_{n\ge1}\{y:P^n(y,C)>0\}$ has a member of positive $P(x,\cdot)$-mass; integrating the corresponding positive function gives $P^{n+1}(x,C)>0$, a contradiction. Thus $P(x,H)=1$ for every $x\in H$. Irreducibility then forces $\phi(H^c)=0$, since no point of $H$ can reach $H^c$; hence $\phi(H)>0$. For every $n\ge1$, invariance and $P^n(x,H)=1$ on $H$ give $\int_{H^c}P^n(x,H)\,\pi(dx)=0$. Irreducibility says every $x\in H^c$ has $P^n(x,H)>0$ for some $n$, so the countable union of these $\pi$-null level sets is $H^c$ and $\pi(H^c)=0$, contradicting $\pi(C)>0$. Therefore $H=\varnothing$. For every state choose $n(x)\ge1$ with $P^{n(x)}(x,C)>0$; then $P^{n(x)+m}(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon P^{n(x)}(x,C)
u(\cdot)$. By [F3], $
u P^t\ge c_t
u$ for every $t\ge N_0$. Choose $L>M+m+N_0$. For every $0\le s\le M$ and $y\in C$, $P^{L-s}(y,\cdot)\ge\epsilon
u P^{L-s-m}(\cdot)\ge\epsilon c_{L-s-m}
u(\cdot).$ The minimum $c>0$ over these finitely many $s$ is positive.

Decompose at the first hitting time $\tau_C=s\le M$. The strong Markov property and step 1.2 give $P^L(x,\cdot)\ge c\nu(\cdot)\Pr_x(\tau_C\le M)\ge cq\nu(\cdot)$ for every $x\in D$. This is one fixed-time minorization, so $D$ is small.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: If $C=\varnothing$, then $PV\le\lambda V$ everywhere. For each integer $N\ge1$, $V_N=V\wedge N$ satisfies $PV_N-V_N\le-(1-\lambda)V$ on $\{V\le N\}$ and $PV_N-V_N\le0$ on $\{V>N\}$. Invariance for the bounded function $V_N$ gives integral zero, so $\pi(\{V\le N\})=0$. Since $V$ is finite-valued, these sets increase to the whole space, contradicting that $\pi$ is a probability. Thus no invariant probability exists in the empty-set case, and the implication is vacuous. Assume $C\ne\varnothing$ below.

Set $V_N=V\wedge N$. Since $V_N\le V$ and $V_N\le N$, $PV_N\le \min(PV,N)$. On $C$, $PV_N-V_N\le\lambda\sup_CV+b$. On $C^c\cap\{V\le N\}$ it is at most $-(1-\lambda)V$, and on $C^c\cap\{V>N\}$ it is at most zero.
Invariance for bounded $V_N$ gives $\int(PV_N-V_N)d\pi=0$. Using the three pointwise bounds from step 1.2, $(1-\lambda)\int_{C^c\cap\{V\le N\}}V\,d\pi\le(\lambda\sup_CV+b)\pi(C)\le\lambda\sup_CV+b.$

The domains $C^c\cap\{V\le N\}$ increase to $C^c$; monotone convergence bounds $\int_{C^c}Vd\pi$ by the right side divided by $1-\lambda$. The integral over $C$ is at most $\sup_CV$. Hence $\pi V<\infty$.

citations.quote:
A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

If $\mu(X)<\infty$ and an algebra $\mathcal C$ of subsets of X generates $\mathcal A$, then for every $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C\in\mathcal C$ with $\mu(E\mathbin\triangle C)<\varepsilon$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\eta=\phi^{\otimes3}(E)>0$. The product measure is finite because $\phi$ is finite. By [F1], the union of the algebras of increasing finite tensor-product partitions is an algebra generating the product sigma-algebra. Apply [F2] to obtain a member $H$ of that algebra with $\phi^{\otimes3}(E\mathbin\triangle H)<\eta/6$. Then $\phi^{\otimes3}(H)>5\eta/6$ and $\phi^{\otimes3}(H\setminus E)<\eta/6<\phi^{\otimes3}(H)/4$, so $E$ occupies more than three quarters of $H$. The set $H$ is a finite union of tensor cells at a common partition level. If every positive-measure cell had occupancy at most three quarters, finite additivity would give the same upper bound on $H$, a contradiction. Thus some cell $U\times V\times W$ has positive product measure and $\phi^{\otimes3}(E\cap(U\times V\times W))>\tfrac34\phi(U)\phi(V)\phi(W)>0$. Only one finite-algebra approximant and one cell of its finite partition are selected; no conditional-expectation representative or choice axiom is used.

Since $E\subseteq A\times_{\!y}B$, Tonelli gives $\int_{U\times V}1_A(x,y)\,d\phi(x)d\phi(y)>\tfrac34\phi(U)\phi(V),$ and likewise $\int_{V\times W}1_B(y,z)\,d\phi(y)d\phi(z)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\phi(W)$. Consequently the sets $C=\{x\in U:\phi(A_1(x)\cap V)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\}$ and $D=\{z\in W:\phi(B_2(z)\cap V)>\tfrac34\phi(V)\}$ have positive measure; otherwise the corresponding integral could not exceed three quarters of the rectangle measure.

For $x\in C$ and $z\in D$, both sections occupy more than three quarters of $V$. The complement of their intersection in $V$ is the union of two sets, each of measure less than $\phi(V)/4$. Thus $\phi(A_1(x)\cap B_2(z))\ge\phi(V)/2>0$. Set $\gamma=\phi(V)/2$.
